hypothesis: UET is a synthesis theory and must choose which standard principle to borrow for how fast a larger system innovates. Bettencourt et al. (2007, PNAS 104, 7301; SFI): innovation output scales as N^beta with beta = 1.27 (new patents), so growth reaches a finite-time singularity that a new innovation resets, giving intervals Delta t ~ N^-(beta-1) (slope -0.27). Kremer (1993, QJE 108, 681): invention rate proportional to population, Delta t ~ N^-1 (slope -1). The card asks which slope the history of lighting technologies supports. It is not a UET-distinct prediction; it decides which borrowed principle the synthesis should use.

observable.quantity: slope b of log10 Delta t on log10 N (Delta t: years between successive lighting introductions; N: world population at the start of each interval)
observable.domain: 11 introductions from Nordhaus (1997) Table 1.1, 3000 BC to the 1980s; 10 intervals

prediction_method.description: Ordinary least squares of log10 Delta t on log10 N with a Student t 95 percent interval (n - 2 dof); population interpolated log-linearly between listed years.

fixed_parameters: primary list of 11 introductions and the reasons for each excluded row, fixed in the script before the run
world population, not the population of the inventing country (AI choice)
lighting as a proxy for innovation in general (AI choice)
beta = 1.27 from Bettencourt et al. 2007 (new patents); Kremer slope -1
pass_criterion: PASS (for beta = 1.27) if the 95 percent interval of b contains -0.27 and does not contain -1.
fail_criterion: FAILED (for beta = 1.27) if the 95 percent interval of b does not contain -0.27; INCONCLUSIVE otherwise.
note: Disclosure: not blind. The AI read both tables while transcribing and registering them and knows from memory roughly when these technologies arrived and how world population grew (intervals shrink from about a thousand years to a few decades while population grows about a hundredfold), so it expects a slope much steeper than -0.27; this expectation favours FAILED for beta = 1.27. No slope was computed before drafting. Bettencourt et al. model cities, not the world; a FAILED result applies to this card's scope (world population, lighting), not to urban scaling as such. The family-first variant is reported only. Proposal with the reasoning: topics/0.25_Strategy_Power_Economics/Doc/PROPOSAL_T024_INNOVATION_INTERVAL_2026-11-18.md.
